en.title: Igbo: the whole course
en.short: What Igbo studies covers, how the degree is organised, its main areas and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Igbo is a language of south-eastern Nigeria and one of Nigeria’s major languages. It belongs to the Igboid group of the Niger-Congo family. This degree studies the language itself, its linguistics, its literature and the culture of its speakers. It trains students to describe the language, analyse texts and discuss culture with evidence. The subject is therefore both a language course and a humanities course. You learn to use Igbo and to study it. The notes are in English. Igbo words appear only where their spelling and tone marks can be given accurately.

Standard Igbo is the standard variety, used in education, media and some publishing. It is not the only form of the language. Dialects differ in sound, vocabulary and tone, and the course treats them as part of the subject, not as mistakes.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text:
In Nigeria, common awards are BA Igbo and BEd Igbo. A full-time first degree usually takes four years, but entry requirements, course codes and lengths differ by institution. Check your own handbook and current regulations. Some universities teach Igbo within linguistics, African studies or education. Outside Nigeria, Igbo is often studied within African studies, linguistics or language programmes, and the award varies.

Education degrees may include teaching practice and curriculum studies. Language degrees may include more literature and linguistics. Read the list of required courses, not only the degree title. Postgraduate study usually leads to MA and PhD awards, but titles and structures differ. A master’s may be coursework and dissertation, or research only. Always confirm the current structure with the department.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The introduction stage builds foundations: the language family and dialects, orthography and tone marking, phonetics, basic grammar, vocabulary and dictionary skills, introductions to oral and written literature, culture and society, and methods of language study and fieldwork. This stage is not optional background; later courses assume it.

The core stage has three strands. Linguistics covers phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics and pragmatics, dialectology and historical linguistics, sociolinguistics and media, lexicography and corpus work, translation and interpreting, and stylistics and discourse. Literature covers oral forms and performance, prose fiction, poetry, drama and theatre, and criticism and theory. Culture, policy and research cover worldview, education and language policy, and research methods with the final year project.

At master’s level, students typically take advanced phonology and morphosyntax, advanced literary theory, language planning and revitalisation, and advanced research methods with dissertation design. The order matters: description before theory, and primary texts before criticism.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Start with sounds and tone. Learn to read and write tone marks and special letters accurately, because errors change meaning. Use a reputable dictionary and copy examples exactly. Read Igbo texts aloud and record yourself. Make a glossary of technical terms and write short definitions in your own words. Set a weekly reading and listening routine. Keep a notebook of examples from real speech, radio, film and social media, with the source and date.

For literature, read the primary text before you read criticism. For fieldwork, ask permission, explain your purpose, record carefully and follow your institution’s ethics rules. Compare dialects, but label each example with its dialect. Revise terms with concrete examples.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Common mistakes include ignoring tone marks or special letters, treating Standard Igbo as the only correct Igbo, and mixing dialect examples without labels. Some students memorise criticism without reading the literary text, or confuse oral performance with written text. Others use outdated policy facts or make a universal rule from one dialect. Do not invent Igbo spellings or tone marks. If you cannot verify a form, describe it in English or mark it as uncertain.

In research, weak sampling and unclear methods are frequent. In exams, answer the question asked and give examples. Check current official sources for education and language policy.

keyPoints: Igbo studies combines language, linguistics, literature and culture.
Standard Igbo is a standardised variety, not the whole language.
Tone and orthography are central from the first year.
Literature courses require reading the primary texts.
Degree lengths and awards differ by country and institution.
Label dialect examples and check current policy sources.

en.title: The Igbo Language: Family, Dialects and Standard Igbo
en.short: Igbo in Niger-Congo, its dialect clusters, and the growth of Standard Igbo.

sections.heading: Igbo in Niger-Congo
sections.text: Igbo is a language of south-eastern Nigeria. It belongs to the Niger-Congo family, in the Volta-Niger branch and the Igboid group. Niger-Congo is one of the world’s largest language families by number of languages. Igbo is not a Bantu language, though both are Niger-Congo. It is related to other Volta-Niger languages but is distinct from them. Many Igbo speakers also use English and Nigerian Pidgin, so multilingualism is common.

sections.heading: Dialects and variation
sections.text: Igbo is not one uniform speech form. It forms a dialect continuum: neighbouring varieties shade into one another, and varieties far apart may be hard to understand. Scholars group the dialects differently, and no single list is agreed. Commonly cited clusters include Onitsha, Nsukka, Owerri, Umuahia and Ngwa. Variation appears in pronunciation, tone, vocabulary and grammar. For example, a household item may have different names in two areas, and a different tone can change a word’s meaning.

sections.heading: How Standard Igbo grew
sections.text: Written Igbo began in the 19th century through missionary and educational work, and early texts reflected local dialects. In the 20th century, committees, writers and language bodies worked towards a common written form. Standard Igbo draws mainly on central dialects, especially Owerri and Umuahia, with contributions from other areas. It is used in schools, media and literature. It is a taught and written standard, not a replacement for local speech.

sections.heading: Standard and dialects together
sections.text: Standard Igbo gives a shared spelling and grammar for books, examinations and public writing. Local dialects remain strong at home, in markets and in everyday talk. A pupil in Aba may speak a local variety at home and read Standard Igbo at school. Standardisation is ongoing, and usage varies by region, publisher and institution.

keyPoints: Igbo belongs to Niger-Congo, Volta-Niger branch, Igboid group.
Igbo is not Bantu and is distinct from other Volta-Niger languages.
Igbo forms a dialect continuum, and scholars group its dialects differently.
Commonly cited clusters include Onitsha, Nsukka, Owerri, Umuahia and Ngwa.
Standard Igbo developed as a written and taught form, based mainly on central dialects.
Local dialects and Standard Igbo coexist in everyday life.

en.title: Igbo Orthography and Tone Marking
en.short: The Igbo alphabet, special letters, digraphs, spelling rules and Standard Igbo tone marks.

sections.heading: Alphabet and special letters
sections.text:
Igbo uses a Latin-based alphabet of single letters and digraphs. A digraph is two letters written together for one sound. The vowels are a, e, i, ị, o, ọ, u, ụ. Consonants include b, d, f, g, h, j, k, l, m, n, p, r, s, t, v, w, y, z. The digraphs are ch, gb, gh, gw, kp, kw, nw, ny and sh.

The dot below in ị, ọ and ụ marks a different vowel, so leaving it out is an error. Letters q and x are not used; c appears only in ch. In alphabet order each digraph counts as one letter.

sections.heading: Spelling rules
sections.text:
Igbo spelling is largely phonemic: one letter or digraph stands for one sound. Write the sounds in order and do not add letters that are not pronounced. Use the correct special vowel wherever it is needed. Keep digraphs whole; do not split ch, gb or nw into separate letters. Avoid English habits such as silent letters or doubled consonants unless a dictionary shows them.

Copy from a reliable Standard Igbo dictionary or textbook. Check every special letter and tone mark, then read the word aloud against the model.

sections.heading: Tone marks
sections.text:
Igbo is a tone language: pitch on a syllable can change meaning. Standard Igbo recognises high and low tones, and downstep. In teaching texts and dictionaries, high tone is marked with an acute accent (á) and low tone with a grave accent (à). Downstep marking varies between sources, so follow the dictionary you use.

Tone marks are part of accurate spelling in dictionaries and language teaching. Many everyday texts omit them, but a first-year student should mark them in assessed writing. Practice by copying a short dictionary entry, marking each vowel, then reading it aloud.

keyPoints: Standard Igbo uses single letters and fixed digraphs such as ch, gb, gh, gw, kp, kw, nw, ny and sh.
The dot below in ị, ọ and ụ marks a different vowel and must not be omitted.
Igbo spelling is largely phonemic, so write letters for sounds and keep digraphs whole.
High tone is marked with an acute accent (á) and low tone with a grave accent (à) in teaching texts and dictionaries.
Downstep marking varies, so follow a reliable Standard Igbo dictionary.
Check special letters and tone marks when copying or writing Igbo for assessment.

en.title: Igbo Phonetics: Sounds and Pronunciation
en.short: How Igbo vowels and consonants are made, described and practised, and why sounds differ from letters.

sections.heading: Sounds and letters
sections.text:
Phonetics studies speech sounds as physical events. A phoneme is a sound that distinguishes words. A letter is a written sign; the two do not match one to one. In Igbo, one sound may be written with two letters, as in ch, gb, kp, kw, gw, nw, ny and sh. Count sounds by listening and by using the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA), not by counting letters.

Igbo spelling is broadly phonemic, but it uses digraphs and special letters such as ị, ọ and ụ. Igbo is also a tonal language: pitch distinguishes words, so listen for tone as well. Learn each sound from a model speaker.

sections.heading: Vowels
sections.text:
Vowels are voiced sounds made with no major blockage of the breath in the mouth. They carry the syllable. Standard Igbo has eight oral vowels: /i/ i, /ɪ/ ị, /e/ e, /a/ a, /ɔ/ ọ, /o/ o, /ʊ/ ụ and /u/ u.

Describe a vowel by tongue height, tongue backness and lip rounding. /i/ and /ɪ/ are high front, but /ɪ/ is lower; /u/ and /ʊ/ are high back, with /ʊ/ lower. /e/ and /o/ are mid, /a/ is low, and /ɔ/ is low-mid back rounded. Vowels may be nasalised, mainly next to nasal consonants such as m and n.

sections.heading: Consonants
sections.text:
Consonants are made by narrowing or stopping the airflow. Describe them by place, manner and voicing. Place is where the narrowing happens: bilabial (both lips), labiodental (lower lip and upper teeth), alveolar (ridge behind the upper teeth), palatal (tongue against the hard palate), velar (soft palate) and glottal (vocal folds). Manner is how air flows: stop, nasal, fricative, affricate and approximant. Voicing means whether the vocal folds vibrate.

Igbo has labial-velar stops /kp/ and /gb/, made with closures at the lips and soft palate at once. /ch/ is an affricate; /m/ and /n/ are nasals.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.text: Practise minimal pairs: words differing in one sound. Contrast i with ị, then u with ụ, keeping the tongue steady. Contrast /kp/ with /gb/ by voicing, and /ch/ with /sh/. Record yourself, compare with a reliable model, and avoid an English-style glide after vowels.

keyPoints: Phonetics studies physical speech sounds; a phoneme distinguishes words, while a letter is a written sign.
Igbo digraphs such as ch, gb, kp and sh show that sounds and letters are not one to one.
Standard Igbo has eight oral vowels: i, ị, e, a, ọ, o, ụ, u.
Vowels are described by tongue height, backness and lip rounding; consonants by place, manner and voicing.
Igbo /kp/ and /gb/ are labial-velar stops made with two closures at once.
Igbo is a tonal language; pitch distinguishes words.
Practise minimal pairs and compare with a reliable model; do not transfer English sounds.

en.title: Basic Igbo Grammar: Words, Phrases and Simple Sentences
en.short: Parts of speech, noun phrases, verb forms and common simple sentence patterns in Standard Igbo.

sections.heading: Words and roles
sections.text: Parts of speech are labels for how words work in a sentence. Igbo grammarians describe nouns (names of people, things and ideas), pronouns (such as I, you, he or she), verbs (actions and states), adjectives, adverbs, conjunctions and particles. The labels are useful but not fixed: a word may act differently in different sentences. Igbo has no grammatical gender and no articles like English 'a' or 'the'; definiteness comes from demonstratives, possessives or context.

sections.heading: Noun phrases
sections.text: A noun phrase is built around a head noun and can act as subject or object. In Igbo, modifiers generally follow the noun: possessive, demonstrative, numeral and adjective. In English gloss, 'my house' is house + my; 'these books’ is books + these. A simple noun phrase may be one noun, one pronoun, or a noun with modifiers. Do not add an English article where Igbo does not use one.

sections.heading: Verb forms
sections.text: A verb root can take tense and aspect markers. Tense places an action in time; aspect shows whether it is complete, ongoing or habitual. Subject pronouns usually come before the verb. The same root changes with different markers, so learn roots with common patterns. In English gloss, 'child eat food' can become 'child is eating food' or 'child ate food' by changing the verb form. Some state verbs, such as be, know or want, behave differently.

sections.heading: Simple sentences
sections.text: Common patterns are subject + verb (intransitive), subject + verb + object (transitive), and identification with a copula-like verb meaning 'be'. The basic order is subject-verb-object. Imperatives use the verb root, sometimes with an object pronoun. To analyse, mark the subject noun phrase, the verb and its markers, then the object. Example: in the English gloss 'child eats food', 'child' is the subject noun phrase, 'eats’ is the verb with present or habitual meaning, and 'food' is the object. If tone marks are missing, ask for a corrected text before deciding meaning.

keyPoints: Parts of speech describe how words function in sentences, not fixed word classes.
A noun phrase has a head noun; modifiers generally follow it in Igbo.
Igbo has no English-style articles; definiteness comes from context and modifiers.
Verb roots combine with tense and aspect markers, and subject pronouns usually precede the verb.
The basic simple sentence order is subject-verb-object; identification uses a verb meaning 'be'.
Tone marks and special letters are part of correct spelling and can change meaning.

en.title: Igbo Vocabulary and Dictionary Skills
en.short: How to record Igbo words, read dictionary entries, sort special letters and choose senses from context.

sections.heading: Building a word list
sections.text:
Vocabulary grows when you meet words in real use and record them at once. Read simple Igbo texts, listen to speech, and note each new word with the sentence where you found it. Group words by theme, such as family or market.

Record the headword with its tone marks and special letters, the part of speech, one clear meaning, an example sentence, and the source. Review often with flashcards. Case: Chidi, a first-year student in Enugu, writes each new word, its tone marks, part of speech, one meaning and one example, then tests himself weekly.

sections.heading: Inside a dictionary entry
sections.text:
A dictionary entry is the whole block for one headword, the word you look up. An Igbo entry often gives the headword with tone marks, the part of speech, and numbered senses. Each sense may have an example sentence. Entries may also show idioms, cross-references and dialect labels.

Read from the top: spelling and tone, then part of speech, then senses. A noun entry will not explain a verb use.

sections.heading: Igbo alphabetical order
sections.text:
Igbo dictionaries follow the Igbo alphabet, not the English one. Digraphs such as ch, gb, kp and kw are treated as single letters. The dotted vowels ị, ọ and ụ, and the nasal ṅ, have their own places. Tone marks are usually ignored when sorting.

So words beginning with ch come after b and before d, not between c and d as in English. When two words look alike, the next letter decides.

sections.heading: Choosing the right sense
sections.text:
Many Igbo words have more than one meaning, listed as numbered senses. To choose, check the part of speech, the words around it, and the topic. Tone can change meaning, so compare the tone marks in the entry with the word in your text.

If a sentence is about farming, choose the farming sense. Read the example under each sense. If no sense fits, the word may be an idiom or a dialect form. Check cross-references or ask a fluent speaker.

keyPoints: Record each new Igbo word with its tone marks, part of speech, one meaning, an example and its source.
Group vocabulary by theme and review it often with flashcards or a notebook.
A dictionary entry gives the headword, tone marks, part of speech, numbered senses and often examples.
Igbo dictionaries sort by the Igbo alphabet; digraphs are single letters and tone marks are usually ignored.
Dotted letters ị, ọ, ụ and nasal ṅ have their own places in alphabetical order.
Choose a sense from context by checking part of speech, nearby words, topic and tone.

en.title: Introduction to Igbo Oral Literature
en.short: This summary covers the main forms of Igbo oral literature, their social functions and the idea of performance.

sections.heading: What oral literature is
sections.text:
Oral literature is verbal art composed and passed on by speech and performance rather than fixed print. In Igbo communities it includes stories, sayings, riddles, songs and praise poems. It is not merely old material: performers reshape it for each occasion, so context, audience and purpose matter.

It is studied through both the words and the occasion of telling.

sections.heading: Main forms
sections.text:
Folktale is a story told for entertainment and teaching; it often has animal tricksters, human heroes and moral endings. Proverb is a short, fixed saying used to support an argument, warn, comfort or criticise with authority. Riddle is a question-and-answer game that tests reasoning, memory and language; it often uses metaphor and wordplay.

Song carries work, ceremony, mourning, satire and protest, often with call-and-response; songs mark births, marriages, funerals and festivals. Praise poetry names and celebrates a person, lineage or achievement, and can also advise or criticise.

sections.heading: Performance and audience
sections.text:
Performance means the live occasion of telling, singing or reciting before an audience. The teller uses voice, gesture, pause, repetition and formulaic openings; the audience answers, claps, sings or corrects. The performer may invite a known audience member to answer.

A folktale told at a village evening, with a chorus answering the opening and a riddle contest before it, is a different event each time. The same story changes with the teller and audience.

sections.heading: Social functions
sections.text:
These forms teach values, preserve history and language, settle disputes, entertain and bind groups. They also transmit language and memory to children.

A proverb may end a family argument; a work song coordinates labour; praise poetry honours a title-holder and reminds him of duty. Because oral literature is public, it can also criticise power indirectly. Recordings and transcripts help study it, but they cannot replace the live occasion.

keyPoints: Igbo oral literature includes folktale, proverb, riddle, song and praise poetry.
Oral literature lives in performance, where teller and audience shape each occasion.
Folktales teach and entertain, proverbs support argument and authority, and riddles test reasoning and language.
Songs carry work, ceremony, mourning, satire and protest, often through call-and-response.
Praise poetry celebrates a person or lineage and can also advise or criticise.
These forms preserve language, history and values and help settle disputes and bind groups.

en.title: Introduction to Written Igbo Literature
en.short: Genres of written Igbo literature and key terms for reading prose, poetry and drama.

sections.heading: Three main genres
sections.text: Written Igbo literature has three genres: prose, poetry and drama. A genre is a recognised kind of writing with its own conventions. Prose tells a story in sentences and paragraphs; it includes the novel and the short story. Poetry arranges language in lines and stanzas and often uses rhythm and imagery. Drama is written to be performed and uses dialogue and stage directions. Written Igbo literature includes original works and translations into Igbo.

sections.heading: Reading prose
sections.text: In prose, ask who narrates. The narrator is the voice telling the story; point of view is the position from which it is told, such as first person (“I”) or third person (“he” or “she”). Plot is the sequence of events; conflict is the struggle that drives it. Setting is time and place. Character is a person in the story; characterisation is how the writer builds that person. Theme is a central idea, such as duty or jealousy. Example: a story about a trader in Onitsha who hides a debt from his family. Trace plot, conflict and theme, and note whether the narrator knows the trader’s thoughts.

sections.heading: Reading poetry
sections.text: Poetry is language arranged in lines, often in stanzas (groups of lines). Rhythm is the pattern of beats; in Igbo, tone also matters, so read aloud. Imagery is language that appeals to the senses. A simile compares using “like” or “as”; a metaphor states that one thing is another. Persona is the speaker, not necessarily the poet. Tone is the speaker’s attitude. Ask how line breaks and repetition shape meaning.

sections.heading: Reading drama
sections.text: Drama is for performance. It uses dialogue (speech between characters), monologue (one character speaking), soliloquy (alone on stage) and aside (heard by the audience, not other characters). Stage directions tell actors how to move or speak. Act and scene are units of the play. Conflict and theme work as in prose. Literary analysis asks how form, language and context work together; it does not only summarise. Describe, interpret, evaluate.

keyPoints: Written Igbo literature has three main genres: prose, poetry and drama.
In prose, identify narrator, point of view, plot, conflict, setting, character and theme.
In poetry, read aloud and note line, stanza, rhythm, imagery, simile, metaphor, persona and tone.
In drama, dialogue, monologue, soliloquy, aside and stage directions shape performance.
Literary analysis describes how form and language create meaning; it is more than summary.

en.title: Igbo Culture and Society: An Introduction
en.short: Kinship, age grades, title societies, religion, festivals and values in varied, changing Igbo societies.

sections.heading: Kinship and community
sections.text:
Igbo societies are not one uniform culture. They are many communities with different histories, dialects and local rules. In many places, kinship is the base of social life. Kinship means relationships through descent and marriage. Many Igbo communities are patrilineal, tracing descent through the father’s line, but this is not universal. A lineage is a group of related families that can trace common descent. It shares duties in marriage, burial and dispute settlement.

The extended family and village community matter in many decisions. Councils of elders, women’s groups and age grades may share public work. Age grades are groups of people of roughly the same age who move through life together. They may take a name, build roads or markets, organise festivals and enforce conduct. Exact age ranges and duties vary by community. For example, Ngozi and Chidi, cousins in one village, may belong to different age grades but share lineage duties at a funeral.

sections.heading: Titles and religion
sections.text:
Title societies are graded associations that confer honour, ritual knowledge and duties. Members may gain prestige, mediate disputes and support community projects. Entry rules, costs and ceremonies differ widely, and some titles are open only to men or particular lineages. A title carries obligations, not just status.

Traditional Igbo religion commonly includes belief in a supreme being, lesser deities, ancestors and spirits. Shrines, priests and diviners may serve these powers. Christianity has many adherents today, and a smaller number of people follow Islam. Many families combine faith with traditional practices. Religion shapes values such as respect and hospitality.

sections.heading: Festivals and values
sections.text: Festivals mark planting, harvest, new year or ancestors. New yam festivals are common in many areas, but names, dates and rites vary. They bring kin together and pass on history through music, dance and speech. Values often praised include hospitality, respect for elders, hard work and honesty. Igbo culture changes over time through trade, migration, colonial rule, education and media.

keyPoints: Igbo culture is varied, and local communities differ in kinship, titles, religion and festivals.
Kinship and lineage shape duties in marriage, burial and dispute settlement in many Igbo communities.
Age grades are age-based groups that may organise work, festivals and conduct.
Title societies confer honour and duties, and their rules vary widely.
Traditional religion includes belief in a supreme being, deities, ancestors and spirits; most Igbo today follow Christianity, and a smaller number follow Islam.
Values such as hospitality and respect for elders are ideals, and Igbo culture changes over time.

en.title: Methods of Language Study and Fieldwork
en.short: Describing language, collecting and recording data, transcription, fieldwork ethics and small projects.

sections.heading: Describing a language
sections.text:
A linguistic description is a systematic account of how a language or variety is used, not how it should be used. It may cover sounds, word forms, sentences, meanings or social use. The method follows the question. A library project uses secondary data: published grammars, dictionaries and articles. Fieldwork produces primary data: material you collect from speakers.

Description begins with clear questions and a record of choices. Write down who was studied, where, when and how. This record is the metadata. Without it, notes and recordings lose value.

sections.heading: Collecting data
sections.text:
Elicitation means asking a speaker to produce words, sentences or judgements, often from a word list or picture task. An interview is a planned conversation; a semi-structured interview has set questions but allows follow-up. Participant observation means joining an activity, such as a market, and taking field notes.

Choose speakers who vary in age, sex, occupation and location, not only friends. Suppose a student studies how traders in Onitsha ask for prices. She records five consenting traders in different stalls, notes the setting and keeps her questions. Five people form a small case study, not a representative sample, so she says so.

sections.heading: Recording and transcription
sections.text:
Record in a quiet place, test the device and make a backup. Label each file with date, place and speaker code. Transcription turns speech into writing. An orthographic transcription uses normal spelling; a phonetic transcription uses the International Phonetic Alphabet to show pronunciation. For Igbo, check tone marks and special letters carefully.

Transcribe a short passage first, then check it with the speaker. Mark pauses, laughter and unclear words. Do not silently correct grammar. Keep the original recording, because a transcript is always a selection.

sections.heading: Ethics and projects
sections.text: Obtain informed consent: explain the purpose, recording, storage and use. Participation must be voluntary, and speakers may withdraw. Anonymise names unless permission is given. Store files securely. Check your department’s current ethics rules before starting.

keyPoints: A linguistic description records how a variety is used and states its methods and metadata.
Primary data come from speakers; secondary data come from published sources.
Elicitation, interviews and participant observation are complementary fieldwork methods.
Choose a varied small sample and report its limits honestly.
Transcription is selective; check tone marks and special letters with the speaker.
Informed consent, voluntary participation, anonymisation and secure storage are basic ethics.

en.title: Igbo Phonology: Tone, Syllable Structure and Vowel Harmony
en.short: Tone, syllable shapes, vowel harmony and phonological rules in Igbo sound analysis.

sections.heading: Tone as meaning
sections.text:
Tone is the use of pitch on a syllable to distinguish words and grammar. Igbo has high and low tones, and downstep, where a high tone is pronounced lower than an earlier high tone. Tone is not stress: it can change the word itself, not just emphasise it.

Two words that share the same consonants and vowels but differ in tone form a minimal pair. In Igbo such pairs are common, so a tone-marked dictionary is essential. Tone can also mark grammatical distinctions such as tense, aspect, possession, negation or question type. The exact patterns vary by dialect and by grammatical construction.

sections.heading: Syllable structure
sections.text:
The common syllable shapes in Standard Igbo are V (a vowel alone), CV (consonant plus vowel) and N (a syllabic nasal). A syllabic nasal is a nasal consonant that carries its own tone and forms a syllable. Consonant clusters are not typical.

The syllabic nasal often assimilates to the place of the following consonant: it becomes labial before a labial, alveolar before an alveolar, and velar before a velar. This is assimilation, where a sound becomes more like a neighbour. Nasal vowels also occur, but their analysis varies. Check a grammar for the dialect you are studying.

sections.heading: Vowel harmony and rules
sections.text:
Vowel harmony is a rule that makes vowels in a word share a feature. In Igbo this feature is often analysed as advanced tongue root (ATR), the position of the tongue root. The +ATR set is usually given as i, e, o, u; the -ATR set as ị, a, ọ, ụ. Most words use vowels from one set, and affixes harmonise with the root.

In many analyses /a/ is neutral and can occur with either set; other analyses treat it as -ATR. Other rules include tone spreading, vowel deletion and glide formation. To analyse a form, propose an underlying representation, state the rule, and derive the surface form. Test it against minimal pairs and check dialect variation.

keyPoints: Tone in Igbo uses pitch to distinguish words and grammatical forms, not merely to add emphasis.
High and low tones are basic; downstep is a lowered high tone and a standard feature of Igbo.
Common syllable shapes are V, CV and syllabic N; consonant clusters are not typical.
A syllabic nasal often assimilates to the place of articulation of the following consonant.
Igbo vowel harmony is commonly analysed as grouping vowels by advanced tongue root, with /a/ often neutral.
Phonological analysis moves from underlying form through a stated rule to the surface form, checking dialect variation.

en.title: Igbo Morphology and Word Formation
en.short: Morphemes, roots, affixes, reduplication, compounding and how to analyse Igbo words.

sections.heading: Morphemes and roots
sections.text:
A morpheme is the smallest unit of meaning. A free morpheme can stand alone as a word; a bound morpheme must attach to something else. The root is the core that carries the main meaning, and an affix is a bound morpheme added to it. A prefix comes before the root and a suffix after it. An allomorph is a variant form of the same morpheme in different sound environments.

Inflectional affixes change a word’s grammar, like English plural -s. Igbo has fewer inflectional suffixes than English. Much grammatical work is done by tone, by auxiliaries and by word order, so do not expect Igbo to copy English patterns.

sections.heading: Affixes and reduplication
sections.text:
Derivational affixes make new words. Igbo uses prefixes to build nouns from verbs and to group nouns into classes. The exact prefixes differ between dialects, so check the standard form in a dictionary.

Reduplication repeats a root or part of it. It can mark emphasis, repetition or intensity, and it often produces new nouns or adjectives. The meaning depends on the particular word, so learn each case instead of applying one rule everywhere.

sections.heading: Compounding and other ways
sections.text:
A compound joins two or more roots into one word with a meaning of its own. The parts may keep their meaning or shift it. Igbo also forms words by borrowing from other languages, by extending the meaning of an existing word, and by shortening descriptive phrases into single words.

Tone carries meaning in Igbo. A change of tone can change a word, so write tone marks whenever you cite a form.

sections.heading: Analysing a word
sections.text:
Write the word and mark the tones. Cut it into morphemes one at a time and label each as root, prefix, suffix or reduplicated part. State the rule in order: which affix attaches to which base, and what word class results.

Test the analysis by finding the same morphemes in other words. If a cut leaves a piece with no meaning and no grammatical job, the cut is probably wrong.

keyPoints: A morpheme is the smallest unit of meaning; a root is the core meaning carrier.
Free morphemes stand alone; bound morphemes must attach to a base.
An allomorph is a variant form of one morpheme in a particular sound environment.
Reduplication repeats a root and may mark emphasis, repetition or intensity.
A compound joins roots into one word with its own meaning.
Test any morpheme analysis by finding the same morphemes in other words.

en.title: Igbo Syntax and Sentence Structure
en.short: Phrase structure, clause and sentence types, verb forms and argument structure in Igbo.

sections.heading: Phrase structure
sections.text:
Syntax studies how words combine into phrases and sentences. A phrase is built around a head: a noun phrase (NP) has a noun head, a verb phrase (VP) has a verb, and a prepositional phrase (PP) has a preposition. Phrases nest.

In a basic Igbo declarative clause the order is subject-verb-object (SVO). Modifiers such as adjectives usually follow the noun. To analyse, bracket phrases and label heads: [NP the child] [VP saw [NP the dog]].

sections.heading: Clauses and sentences
sections.text:
A clause has a subject and a predicate. A main clause can stand alone; a subordinate clause depends on it. Sentences are simple (one main clause), compound (two main clauses) or complex (main plus subordinate).

Igbo sentences can be declarative, interrogative or imperative, and each can be positive or negative. Yes/no questions often use a question particle or tone; content questions use interrogative words. Negation uses negative markers, and tone can change meaning. Speakers may front a topic or focus phrase; this changes information structure, not basic clause type.

sections.heading: Verbs and arguments
sections.text:
The verb is the centre of the clause. Igbo verbs mark tense and aspect through particles and auxiliaries, and tone can distinguish forms. Argument structure is the set of participants a verb requires. Valency describes how many: intransitive takes one argument, transitive two, ditransitive three.

Roles include agent (doer), patient (affected) and recipient. Serial verb constructions join two or more verbs under one subject to express sequence, purpose or cause. Adjuncts add time, place or manner but are not required. To analyse, identify the verb, count its arguments, assign roles, then note any fronted topic or focus.

sections.heading: Worked case
sections.text:
Take a clause meaning 'the child saw the dog' (shown here as an English gloss). Bracket it: [NP the child] [VP saw [NP the dog]]. Saw is transitive: subject is agent, object is patient.

Igbo normally uses this SVO order. Fronting 'the dog' puts it in focus, and the rest of the clause comments on it.

keyPoints: Basic Igbo declarative clauses normally follow subject-verb-object order.
A phrase is built around a head: noun in NP, verb in VP, preposition in PP.
Igbo verbs mark tense and aspect with particles and auxiliaries, and tone can distinguish forms.
Argument structure is the set of participants a verb requires; valency can be intransitive, transitive or ditransitive.
Serial verb constructions combine verbs under one subject to express sequence, purpose or cause.
Topic and focus fronting are grammatical choices about information structure, not errors.

en.title: Igbo Semantics and Pragmatics: Meaning in Use
en.short: Word and sentence meaning, idiom, metaphor, politeness and context-dependent meaning in Igbo.

sections.heading: Semantics and pragmatics
sections.text: Semantics studies conventional meaning: what a word or sentence means apart from a particular occasion. Pragmatics studies meaning in context: what a speaker intends and a hearer infers from situation, relationship and shared knowledge. Sense is a word’s place in the vocabulary; reference is what it points to on a particular occasion. Entailment follows necessarily: if Ada is Chidi’s sister, then Chidi has a sister. Presupposition is background assumed: 'Ada stopped singing' assumes she sang before.

sections.heading: Word, sentence, idiom, metaphor
sections.text: At word level, denotation is core meaning and connotation is the feeling a word carries. Synonymy, antonymy, hyponymy and polysemy name meaning relations: sameness, oppositeness, inclusion of meaning, and one word with several related senses. Sentence meaning is built compositionally from words and grammar, but idioms are fixed expressions whose meaning is not the sum of their parts, so they are learned whole. Metaphor maps one domain onto another and is not mere decoration. In Igbo, as in other languages, idioms and proverbs often depend on shared cultural knowledge, so word-for-word translation can mislead.

sections.heading: Politeness and context
sections.text: Pragmatics explains how one sentence can perform different acts. A speech act is what an utterance does, such as request, promise, apology or warning. Politeness concerns face, a person’s wish to be approved and not imposed on. Igbo speakers may signal politeness through titles, kinship terms, greetings, indirectness and attention to age or status, though usage varies by place and family. Deixis is meaning that depends on context, as with pronouns and words for here, now and tomorrow. Case: Ada tells a guest, 'There is cold water in the fridge.' The words state a fact; in context they may be an offer. To analyse meaning in use, record speaker, hearer, setting, relationship and earlier talk. Give a literal paraphrase, then a likely inference, and test it against the hearer’s response. Distinguish what is said from what is implied, and describe Igbo evidence before comparing it with English categories.

keyPoints: Semantics studies conventional word and sentence meaning; pragmatics studies meaning in context.
Sense is a word’s place in the vocabulary; reference is what it points to on a particular occasion.
Entailment follows necessarily from a sentence; presupposition is background assumed.
Idioms are fixed expressions learned whole, and metaphors map one domain onto another.
Politeness involves face and may be shown through titles, kinship terms, greetings and indirectness.
Analyse meaning in use by recording context and separating what is said from what is implied.

en.title: Igbo Dialectology, Historical and Comparative Linguistics
en.short: Dialect variation, Standard Igbo, internal reconstruction, Igboid comparison and theories of Igbo origins.

sections.heading: Dialect variation and attitudes
sections.text: Igbo is a dialect continuum: neighbouring varieties are mutually intelligible, but distant ones may not be. Linguists group varieties by region, such as Onitsha, Nsukka, Owerri and Ngwa, but boundaries are not sharp. Speakers may treat their own variety as true Igbo and others as different. Standard Igbo carries prestige in schools and media, while local dialects mark identity. These attitudes affect which forms are called correct.

sections.heading: Standard Igbo
sections.text: Standard Igbo is a written and taught variety. It grew from Central Igbo, which drew mainly on dialects around Owerri and Umuahia, and later committees adjusted it. It is not neutral: speakers from other areas may find it close to, or distant from, their own speech. Problems include tone marking, spelling choices, lexical gaps and the belief that the standard favours one region. It helps communication across regions but can weaken local varieties if they are not used in school or media.

sections.heading: Reconstruction and comparison
sections.text: Internal reconstruction uses alternations inside one language to suggest earlier forms. A simple English example is sing, sang, sung, which suggests an older vowel pattern. The comparative method compares related languages to reconstruct a common ancestor, called a proto-language. For Igbo, scholars compare Igboid languages, the branch of Niger-Congo that includes Igbo and its closest relatives, such as Ekpeye, Ikwerre and Ogba. Igbo itself contains dialect clusters, such as Ezaa-Izi-Ikwo-Mgbo. Classification varies: some varieties are called dialects by some scholars and languages by others. Regular sound correspondences, not looks alone, support a claim of relationship.

sections.heading: Origins and spread
sections.text: Theories of Igbo origins and spread differ. Some place early Igbo speech in the Nsukka, Udi and Owerri area; others argue for movement from the Niger-Benue confluence or from the east. Oral traditions, archaeology and linguistics each give partial evidence. The Igbo-Ukwu finds show an early complex society, but they do not identify the language spoken. The spread of Igbo is often linked to population movement and trade, but no single account is accepted by all scholars.

keyPoints: Igbo is a dialect continuum, so neighbouring varieties are mutually intelligible while distant ones may not be.
Standard Igbo grew from Central Igbo, which drew mainly on Owerri and Umuahia dialects, and it is not a neutral variety.
Standard Igbo helps cross-regional communication but can weaken local varieties, and it carries prestige in schools and media.
Internal reconstruction uses alternations within one language to suggest earlier forms.
The comparative method reconstructs a proto-language from regular sound correspondences across related languages.
Igboid classification varies, and theories of Igbo origins and spread remain debated.

en.title: Igbo Sociolinguistics, Media and Digital Communication
en.short: How Igbo is used beside English in society, media, social media, software and keyboards.

sections.heading: Language in society
sections.text: Sociolinguistics studies how language varies with setting, class, age and education. A domain is an area of language use, such as home, school, market or radio. In Nigeria, English is the official language and dominates schooling, law and much national media, while Igbo is a major language of the south-east. Many Igbo speakers are bilingual, using two languages, or multilingual. Diglossia is a stable division of roles between two languages or varieties: one for formal public life, another for everyday talk. English often takes formal roles and Igbo everyday ones, but this varies by place and generation.

sections.heading: Switching and borrowing
sections.text: Code-switching is moving between languages within a conversation or sentence. It can mark identity, emphasis or a change of topic. A presenter may read a headline in English, then explain it in Igbo. Borrowing is taking a word from another language and adapting it to one’s own sound and grammar; Igbo has borrowed widely from English, especially in technology and administration. Code-switching is normal in bilingual communities, not laziness. Language shift is the gradual replacement of one language by another across generations, a concern for Igbo in cities and the diaspora.

sections.heading: Media and digital
sections.text: Radio reaches listeners who do not read easily. Igbo radio includes news, phone-ins, drama and adverts, and presenters often mix Igbo with English. Film and video, including Nollywood, use Igbo dialogue, music and proverbs, while subtitles and English titles widen audiences. Media can support the language through consistent spelling and tone marking, but may spread a standard form unlike local speech. Social media and messaging apps give Igbo new written spaces. Users often omit tone marks because keyboards make them slow. Tone marks matter because tone distinguishes words but context usually helps. Unicode lets computers store Igbo letters and tone marks, and a good Igbo keyboard should include them. Localisation means adapting software into Igbo. Machine translation and speech tools are growing but uneven. Digital media connect speakers yet they also favour English.

keyPoints: Sociolinguistics links language use to social setting, identity and power.
Bilingualism is using two languages; diglossia is a stable division of roles between two languages or varieties.
Code-switching is normal in bilingual talk and can signal identity or a change of topic.
Borrowing adapts words from another language into a speaker’s own sound and grammar.
Igbo radio, film and social media extend the language but often mix it with English.
Unicode and good keyboards support written Igbo, including tone marks, but digital tools remain uneven.

en.title: Igbo Lexicography and Corpus Development
en.short: Making and judging Igbo dictionaries, entry structure, definitions, examples and text corpora.

sections.heading: Dictionary making
sections.text: Lexicography is the craft of compiling dictionaries. A lexicographer decides the purpose and users of the dictionary, then collects evidence of how words are used. For Igbo, that evidence must record tone marks and special letters such as ị, ọ, ụ and ṅ where the source uses them. A dictionary may be descriptive, recording usage, or prescriptive, recommending a standard. Most modern dictionaries are mainly descriptive but still label dialect forms and informal words.

sections.heading: Entry structure
sections.text: An entry begins with a headword, also called a lemma, the form used for lookup. It may show pronunciation, tone, part of speech, senses and examples. Each sense is a distinct meaning. A definition should be clear, not circular, and should fit the part of speech. Examples show the word in a natural sentence and should come from recorded usage or be checked by a speaker. A small entry might have: headword, tone pattern, noun, sense 1 with one example, sense 2 with one example, and a dialect label. Cross-references link related words.

sections.heading: Building a corpus
sections.text: A corpus is a large, organised collection of texts used for language study. An Igbo corpus may include novels, newspapers, interviews, proverbs and social media posts, with permission and personal data removed. Builders record metadata such as source, date, place and genre. They transcribe oral material, check spelling and tone, and add annotation, that is, labels such as part of speech. Balance matters: a corpus drawn only from one dialect or one newspaper will mislead.

sections.heading: Using and judging
sections.text: Corpus tools show frequency and concordance, a list of every occurrence of a word in context. These help the lexicographer choose examples, order senses and spot collocations, words that often occur together. To judge a dictionary, ask about coverage, accuracy of tone and diacritics, clarity of definitions, quality of examples, dialect labels, date and evidence. Check several entries against your own knowledge and against a corpus. No dictionary is final; usage changes, so record the edition and date.

keyPoints: Lexicography is the craft of compiling dictionaries from evidence of real usage.
An entry needs a headword, tone and diacritics, part of speech, clear senses, examples and cross-references.
A corpus is an organised, balanced collection of texts with metadata and annotation.
Concordances and frequency lists help lexicographers choose examples, order senses and find collocations.
Judge an Igbo dictionary by coverage, accuracy of tone and diacritics, definitions, examples, dialect labels and date.
Record permissions and remove personal data when building corpora from oral or social media sources.

en.title: Igbo Translation and Interpreting
en.short: Igbo-English translation and interpreting: equivalence, cultural terms, ethics and practice.

sections.heading: Two modes
sections.text: Translation is the written transfer of meaning from a source language (the language translated from) to a target language (the language translated into). Interpreting is the spoken or signed transfer, often in real time. A translator can revise; an interpreter must decide quickly. Modes include consecutive interpreting, where the speaker pauses, simultaneous interpreting, near real time, and liaison interpreting for short turns in meetings. A written health notice needs translation; a live meeting needs interpreting.

sections.heading: Equivalence and culture
sections.text: Equivalence is the closest natural match in meaning, function and tone. It can be formal, close to the source form, or dynamic, aiming at the same effect on the target reader; neither is always right. Cultural terms are words tied to a way of life, such as kinship terms, titles and foods. They often lack a one-word match. Options include keeping the Igbo term with a short gloss (explanation), using a descriptive phrase, a functional equivalent that does the same job, or borrowing. For example, extended family may need a description or a specific lineage term, since Igbo kin terms are more precise than the English. Check every Igbo spelling and tone mark before printing.

sections.heading: Professional ethics
sections.text: Professional ethics are accepted standards of conduct that protect clients and the public. Core duties are competence (accept only work you can do well), accuracy (no additions or omissions that change meaning), confidentiality, impartiality, and declaring conflicts of interest. An interpreter should not give advice or act as an advocate unless the role requires it. Codes vary by country and organisation; check the current code. In legal or medical settings, ask for clarification rather than guess.

sections.heading: Practice routine
sections.text: For a short text, read twice, identify purpose, audience and register (level of formality), list unknown terms, draft, then revise against the source. Check names, numbers, dates and negation (such as not). Back-translation, translating the draft back into the source language, can reveal drift. For interpreting, record short speeches, interpret consecutively, then compare with the original. Keep a glossary of agreed terms.

keyPoints: Translation is written; interpreting is spoken or signed and often immediate.
Equivalence means the closest natural match in meaning, function and tone, not word-for-word copying.
Cultural terms often need a kept term with gloss, a description or a functional equivalent.
Professional ethics require competence, accuracy, confidentiality and impartiality.
Check names, numbers, dates and negation in every draft.
Back-translation and glossaries help catch drift and keep terms consistent.

en.title: Igbo Stylistics and Discourse Analysis
en.short: Style, register, rhetoric, discourse structure and text analysis in spoken and written Igbo.

sections.heading: Style and stylistics
sections.text:
Style is the set of choices a speaker or writer makes: word choice, sentence length, tone, imagery and formality. Stylistics studies those choices and their effects. It asks not only what a text says but how saying shapes meaning.

In Igbo, a funeral speech, a radio news item and a friendly message may share grammar but differ in rhythm, repetition, direct address and vocabulary. The analyst describes the pattern, then explains its effect.

sections.heading: Register and rhetoric
sections.text:
Register is the variety used in a particular situation, shaped by topic, audience and relationship. A classroom explanation, a sermon and a market bargain may all be Igbo, yet their register differs in politeness, technical terms and sentence shape. Register is not dialect, which links to place or group.

Rhetorical devices are patterned ways of persuading or holding attention. Examples include repetition, parallelism (balanced phrases), rhetorical questions, direct address, metaphor and proverbs. The analyst names the device, gives context and effect.

sections.heading: Discourse structure
sections.text:
Discourse analysis studies language beyond sentences: how utterances connect into conversations, speeches, stories, notices and arguments. It examines openings, closings, turn-taking, topic development and speaker roles. Cohesion is the formal links, such as pronouns, conjunctions and repeated words. Coherence is the overall sense that the parts belong together.

Genre is a recognised text type with expected moves. A meeting notice may move from purpose to date, place and contact. A narrative may move from setting to complication and resolution. These are tendencies, not fixed laws.

sections.heading: A short analysis
sections.text:
Take a village meeting announcement, spoken and printed. The spoken version may open with a greeting, repeat the date, and use direct address. The printed notice may use a heading, short lines and a contact name. Compare these choices and their fit to audience and purpose.

A method is: describe the context, mark text boundaries, list cohesive links, identify register and rhetorical devices, then explain effects. Check claims against the text. If a feature is uncertain, say so.

keyPoints: Stylistics analyses the choices that create style and their effects in context.
Register is the situation-bound variety of language, not the same as dialect.
Discourse analysis studies how sentences combine into coherent texts and talk.
Cohesion uses formal links such as pronouns and conjunctions; coherence is the overall sense of unity.
Rhetorical devices include repetition, parallelism, rhetorical questions, direct address, metaphor and proverbs.
A sound analysis describes context, boundaries, links, register and devices, then checks claims against the text.

en.title: Igbo Oral Literature: Forms and Performance
en.short: Forms, performance, audience, transmission, and methods for collecting and analysing Igbo oral texts.

sections.heading: Forms and functions
sections.text:
Igbo oral literature is composed and carried in speech and performance, not fixed in writing. Its main forms are the folktale, a narrative told to entertain and teach; the proverb, a short fixed saying used to sum up experience or settle an argument; the riddle, a puzzle with accepted answers; song; praise poetry, honouring a person, lineage or deity; and oral narrative, longer accounts of history, heroes or origins. Forms overlap: a folktale may contain songs, and a praise poem may use proverbs.

Each form has rules and occasions. A proverb works when speaker and hearer share the situation it points to. A praise poem may be sung at a title ceremony or funeral. The same story teaches conduct and shared values.

sections.heading: Performance and audience
sections.text:
Performance is not decoration added to a finished text; it is how the text exists. The teller uses voice, gesture, expression, pauses, repetition and sometimes dance or instruments. Audience members may answer in chorus, laugh, correct a mistake, ask for a repeat or supply a line. Each performance is a version, not a copy.

Transmission is mainly by word of mouth through families, age groups, festivals, religious occasions and specialist performers. Because memory and occasion change, variants are normal. A good study treats variants as evidence of skill, audience and setting, not as errors. The audience is co-performer and judge.

sections.heading: Collecting and analysing
sections.text:
Field collection should record the text and its context. Note the date, place, language variety, performer, audience and occasion. Ask permission, explain the use of the recording, and credit the performer. Record audio where possible, then transcribe carefully, marking tone and special letters, and translate without hiding uncertain lines.

Analysis asks about form, structure, formulaic phrases, imagery, function and performance. Compare versions from different tellers. For example, two recordings of one folktale may differ in length and song because one teller had a lively audience. The difference is data about performance, not proof that one text is false.

keyPoints: Igbo oral literature exists in performance, so each telling is a version rather than a fixed copy.
The main forms include folktale, proverb, riddle, song, praise poetry and oral narrative.
The audience helps shape the performance through responses and requests.
Transmission is mainly oral, through families, festivals, age groups and specialist performers.
Field collection must record context, seek permission and credit performers.
Analysis compares form, function, performance and variants, not just words on a page.

en.title: The Igbo Novel and Short Story
en.short: Development, narrative technique, character, setting and theme in Igbo prose fiction.

sections.heading: Beginnings and growth
sections.text: Igbo prose fiction means novels and short stories written in Igbo. It grew from oral storytelling and early mission literacy. Omenuko by Pita Nwana (1933) is commonly named as the first Igbo novel. Later fiction widened to social change, war, migration and city life. Short stories appeared in magazines, school readers and anthologies. Accounts of firsts and dates vary, so check your sources.

sections.heading: Narrative technique
sections.text: Narrative technique is how a story is told. The narrator may speak in the first person (I) or third person (he, she, they). An omniscient narrator knows all; limited focalisation stays inside one character’s knowledge. Igbo prose often uses proverbs, dialogue, repetition and oral formulas. In an invented story, a third-person narrator stays inside Chidi’s mind as he refuses to help his cousin Emeka; a later sentence reveals Emeka’s child is ill. The technique pushes readers to judge Chidi.

sections.heading: Character and setting
sections.text: Characterisation builds people through action, speech, description and other characters’ views. A round character is complex and can change; a flat character is one-dimensional and stays fixed. Setting is time, place and social rules: village, market, church, school or city. In the Chidi example, the market town and strong kinship duty make the refusal a moral conflict, not mere stinginess. Setting can carry theme. It shapes what characters can do and what readers expect.

sections.heading: Theme and close reading
sections.text: Theme is a central idea, such as kinship, morality, colonial change, religion, gender, corruption or migration. Do not reduce a story to one lesson. Close reading means slow attention to a short passage: who speaks, diction, tone, images, proverbs and sentence rhythm. Ask how form supports theme. Short stories compress conflict and often turn at the end; novels develop subplots and many characters. Compare passages across a writer’s work.

keyPoints: Igbo prose fiction includes novels and short stories written in Igbo, shaped by oral narrative and literacy.
Omenuko by Pita Nwana (1933) is commonly named the first Igbo novel.
Narrative technique covers narrator, point of view, focalisation, chronology and use of proverbs and dialogue.
Characterisation and setting work together to make moral and social conflict believable.
Theme is a central idea, not a simple moral; close reading shows how language and form create it.
Short stories compress conflict, while novels develop subplots and wider social worlds.

en.title: Igbo Poetry: Form, Tone and Close Reading
en.short: Written Igbo poetry, form, imagery, rhythm, tone, oral roots and close reading.

sections.heading: Written and oral
sections.text:
Written Igbo poetry is composed for the page, but it grows from oral poetry: song, praise, lament, proverb and story performed before listeners. Oral poetry lives in performance, with voice, gesture and audience response.

Written poetry keeps some features, such as refrain (a repeated line) and direct address, but it can also be silent and private on the page. A poet may imitate a performer’s voice without an actual performer.

sections.heading: Form, rhythm, tone
sections.text:
Form is the poem’s shape: line, stanza, refrain and overall pattern. Some Igbo poems use regular stanzas and refrains; others use free verse, which has no fixed metre (a set sound pattern).

Rhythm is the felt movement of the poem. In Igbo it can come from syllable count, line length, repetition, parallelism (balanced phrasing) and tone patterns. Tone matters because Igbo is tonal: pitch helps carry meaning, and the same written letters can stand for different words with different tones. Standard written Igbo usually leaves tone unmarked and adds marks only where they are needed to avoid confusion. Read aloud and listen for the poem’s own beat.

sections.heading: Imagery and close reading
sections.text:
Imagery is language that appeals to the senses or creates a picture. Metaphor calls one thing another; simile compares with 'like' or 'as'; personification gives human qualities to non-human things. A symbol is an image with a larger meaning, such as a market for social life. Tone also means the speaker’s attitude, such as grief, mockery or praise.

Read the poem aloud. Identify the persona (the voice speaking, not necessarily the poet), the situation and the addressee. Notice repetition, contrasts, line breaks and where the refrain falls. For a hypothetical couplet, 'The rain has come; / the market is quiet', ask who speaks, what the rain means, and why quiet follows. Support every answer with words from the poem, not guesswork. This is close reading.

keyPoints: Written Igbo poetry draws on oral poetry but is composed for the page.
Form includes line, stanza, refrain and overall pattern; free verse has no fixed metre.
Rhythm in Igbo poetry can come from syllables, repetition, parallelism and tone patterns.
Igbo is tonal, so tone affects meaning; standard written Igbo usually leaves tone unmarked.
Imagery works through metaphor, simile, personification and symbol.
Close reading supports claims with words from the poem, not guesswork.

en.title: Igbo Drama and Theatre
en.short: Written Igbo plays, structure, character, staging, and links between theatre and community ritual.

sections.heading: Drama as text and performance
sections.text: Drama is writing composed for performance; theatre is the event in which actors perform before an audience. A written Igbo play is both a text to read and a script to stage. Reading asks about plot, character, dialogue and theme. Staging asks about voice, movement, costume, props, set, music and audience response. Stage directions are the writer’s instructions about setting, action and tone; they guide a production but do not fix it.

sections.heading: Structure and character
sections.text: Most plays use exposition, which gives background; complication, which creates conflict; climax, the turning point; and resolution, which settles the action. Conflict may be between people, within one person, or between a person and society. The protagonist is the main character; the antagonist opposes the protagonist. Characterisation is built through dialogue, action, what others say, and stage directions. A foil is a character who contrasts with another and so reveals that character more clearly.

sections.heading: Ritual and staging
sections.text:
Igbo theatre has roots in community performance: masquerade, festival, music, dance, storytelling and proverb. Ritual is repeated symbolic action with recognised rules; theatre frames action for an audience. They overlap but are not the same. A masquerade in a festival may be believed to embody a spirit; the same mask on a modern stage is usually a theatrical sign, a performed image rather than a spirit. Written Igbo drama often adapts oral forms, using a narrator, song, call-and-response or a chorus-like group. Scholars disagree on how far theatre grew from ritual; some stress continuity, others stress schools, churches and printing.

Imagine a student play, The New Yam, invented for this note. Ada hides the first yams; her mother warns her; a masquerade enters; Ada confesses and shares. As text, mark exposition, conflict, climax and resolution. As performance, ask how costume, drumming, blocking (the planned movement of actors) and audience reaction change the meaning.

keyPoints: Drama is written for performance; theatre is the performance event.
Dramatic structure usually moves through exposition, complication, climax and resolution.
Characterisation is built by dialogue, action, what others say and stage directions.
Igbo theatre draws on masquerade, festival, music, dance and storytelling.
Ritual and theatre overlap, but ritual aims at symbolic action while theatre frames action for an audience.
In performance analysis, staging choices such as costume, blocking and music shape meaning.

en.title: Literary Criticism and Theory for Igbo Literature
en.short: Critical approaches and the debate on applying Western theory to Igbo oral and written texts.

sections.heading: Main approaches
sections.text: Literary criticism is reasoned interpretation and evaluation. A theory is a set of assumptions that guides the critic’s questions. Formalism, including New Criticism, practises close reading of language and structure. Structuralism looks for underlying patterns, such as repeated functions in tales. Stylistics uses linguistics to describe tone, metaphor and repetition. Reader-response criticism asks how readers or audiences make meaning. Sociological and Marxist criticism examine class, labour and power. Postcolonial criticism examines colonial representation, resistance and hybridity. Feminist criticism examines gender roles. Performance criticism treats oral texts as events shaped by audience, music and gesture.

sections.heading: Applying the approaches
sections.text: Oral texts reward performance criticism: a folktale changes when the audience responds or sings. Formalism can still map its opening, complication and ending. Sociological criticism can ask which values the tale supports. Written Igbo texts need close reading plus context: who publishes, who reads, what history it addresses. A critic should name the approach and show evidence. Do not force a Western category where the text works differently. A novel may not fit the Western idea of a solitary author if it grew from oral performance.

sections.heading: The theory debate
sections.text: Some scholars argue that Western theory carries foreign assumptions and can distort African oral art. The critic Chinweizu and co-authors attacked Eurocentric standards and urged African-centred criticism. Others reply that theory is a tool, not a passport, and that postcolonial theory itself grew from anti-colonial critique. The debate is not settled. A useful test is whether an approach explains the text, respects its language and history, and admits what it leaves out. No single method is prescribed.

sections.heading: A small case
sections.text: Take a folktale about a tortoise, a common trickster figure. A formalist notes repetition and a clear ending. A performance critic notes songs, pauses and audience laughter. A sociological critic asks whether cunning is praised or punished. A postcolonial reading is justified only if colonial experience or its legacy is present. For a written novel, a Marxist reading might examine trade and debt, while a feminist reading examines marriage and authority. The question decides the tool.

keyPoints: Literary criticism interprets and evaluates texts; theory supplies the questions.
Formalist, stylistic, sociological, postcolonial, feminist and performance approaches ask different questions.
Oral texts reward performance criticism because audience, music and gesture shape meaning.
The debate over Western theory in African literature is unresolved; test an approach by its explanatory power and respect for context.
Name the approach you use and support it with evidence from the text.
No approach is neutral: each reveals some features and hides others.

en.title: Igbo Culture and Worldview: Persons, Community and Change
en.short: Igbo ideas of personhood, community, religion, time and ethics, and their variation in language and literature.

sections.heading: Culture as debate
sections.text: Igbo culture is not one fixed system. Igbo-speaking communities differ by locality, history, generation, gender, class, religion and migration. Colonial rule, Christianity, education, trade and diaspora have changed practices. A worldview is a shared set of assumptions about reality, value and action; it is learned and argued over, not simply inherited. Scholars therefore speak of Igbo worldviews in the plural. Ask which community, which period and whose account.

sections.heading: Persons and community
sections.text: Many accounts stress relational personhood: a person becomes fully human through family, age grade, village and moral conduct. This does not erase individual choice. Some traditions emphasise destiny or personal spirit; others stress achievement through titles, marriage, parenthood or service. Community appears in kinship, village assemblies, age grades and title societies, but their power and form vary. A fictional case: Nkiru, a young woman in a town union, gains respect through care for elders and skill in mediation. Her standing is personal and communal at once.

sections.heading: Religion, time, ethics
sections.text: Religion often includes belief in a supreme being, spirits, ancestors and moral powers, but names, rituals and emphasis vary. Christianity is now widespread, and many people combine church life with customary practices; others reject such mixing. Time may be experienced through seasons, markets, festivals and life stages as well as clock time; linear and cyclical views can coexist. Ethics commonly values hospitality, respect, truth, solidarity and restorative settlement, yet these values are debated and sometimes breached.

sections.heading: Reading variation
sections.text: Language and literature show these debates. Proverbs, greetings, names and praise poetry carry ideals; novels, drama and poetry test them against change, gender conflict, migration and faith. Avoid reading one text as the voice of all Igbo people. Compare sources: oral performance, archival records, interviews and fiction. Ask what is being claimed, by whom, for whom, and what alternative accounts exist.

keyPoints: Igbo culture and worldview vary by community, period, generation, gender, class and religion.
Relational personhood means people become fully human through community and moral conduct, without losing individual agency.
Community institutions such as kinship, age grades and village assemblies differ in form and power.
Religious practice often combines belief in a supreme being, spirits and ancestors with Christianity, but individuals differ.
Time and ethics are understood through festivals, life stages, hospitality, respect and restorative settlement, and these ideals are debated.
Language and literature express and contest worldview, so no single text speaks for all Igbo people.

en.title: Igbo in Education and Language Policy
en.short: Teaching Igbo as first and second language, mother-tongue education, curriculum, assessment and Nigerian policy.

sections.heading: Policy in Nigeria
sections.text: Nigeria’s National Policy on Education recommends mother-tongue education in early schooling. Mother-tongue education means teaching through the child’s first language. The policy allows the mother tongue or the language of the immediate community as the medium in pre-primary and early primary. English is taught as a subject, then used more as a medium later. Igbo is one of Nigeria’s major languages and is examined in Nigerian school certificates. Implementation varies, so check the current official policy.

sections.heading: Igbo as first language
sections.text: Teaching Igbo as a first language (L1) means teaching pupils who already speak an Igbo dialect at home. The teacher builds on oral knowledge but must handle the gap between home dialect and standard Igbo. Early work uses listening and speaking. Reading and writing follow, with attention to spelling and tone. Case: Ngozi teaches Primary 2 in Enugu. She accepts pupils’ local forms, then introduces the standard written word in reading. She does not call home speech wrong.

sections.heading: Igbo as second language
sections.text: Teaching Igbo as a second language (L2) means teaching learners whose first language is not Igbo, or who do not speak it at home. The aim is practical communication, not native-like control at first. Lessons move from listening and speaking to reading and writing, using pictures, dialogues and short texts. Grammar is explained in English where needed. In mixed classes, pair work helps stronger speakers support beginners. Assessment should match the level: oral response, matching, dictation and short composition.

sections.heading: Curriculum and assessment
sections.text: A curriculum is the planned content, aims and sequence of a course. An Igbo syllabus usually covers oral work, reading, writing, literature and culture. Assessment means gathering evidence of learning. Formative assessment happens during teaching: questions, observation, class exercises. Summative assessment comes at the end: tests and examinations. A balanced plan tests all four skills. For example, 20 marks for oral interview, 20 for dictation, 30 for comprehension and 30 for composition total 100. Teacher training, textbooks and tone-marked materials remain challenges.

keyPoints: Nigeria’s National Policy on Education recommends mother-tongue education in early schooling, with English taught as a subject and used more as a medium later.
Mother-tongue education means teaching through the child’s first language, often the language of the immediate community.
Teaching Igbo as L1 builds on home dialect but introduces standard Igbo reading and writing.
Teaching Igbo as L2 aims at practical communication and moves from oral work to literacy.
A curriculum sets planned content and sequence, while assessment gathers evidence of learning through formative and summative tasks.
Teacher training, textbooks and tone-marked materials remain practical challenges for Igbo in education.

en.title: Research Methods and the Final Year Project in Igbo Studies
en.short: Designing, sourcing, analysing, writing and defending a small Igbo studies project.

sections.heading: Designing the project
sections.text: A research project starts with a narrow question, not a broad topic. “How do market traders in one town use proverbs?” is workable; “Igbo proverbs” is not. Write a proposal of a few pages: title, background, research question, aims, short literature review, method, ethics, timetable and bibliography. The literature review shows what others have written and where your gap is. Define key terms. Keep the scope small enough for the time and resources you have. A good question can be answered with evidence you can actually collect.

sections.heading: Sources and analysis
sections.text: Secondary sources are published writings about a subject: books, journal articles and theses. Primary sources are first-hand materials you collect or study yourself: interviews, recordings, questionnaires, observation, and the literary texts or archival records you analyse. For oral material, record with permission, then transcribe, which means writing out the speech, including tone marks where you can. Analyse by coding: label repeated ideas, then group them into themes. For literary work, use close reading, a careful study of the text, and compare with other critics. Example: Ngozi studies proverbs in family meetings in one town. She records ten meetings with consent, transcribes them, codes who speaks and when, and compares her findings with published collections. Keep copies of recordings and notes, and store them safely.

sections.heading: Writing and defence
sections.text: Follow your department’s format. A common shape is introduction, literature review, methodology, findings, discussion, conclusion and references. Methodology explains how you collected and analysed data, and its limits. Quote sources honestly and keep a consistent reference style. In the oral defence, summarise your question, method, main findings and limits in a few minutes. Expect questions on your evidence and ethics. Answer calmly; if you do not know, say so. Your supervisor’s advice and the department’s current guide matter more than any general rule. Proofread the final text and check every reference.

keyPoints: A final year project answers a narrow research question, not a broad topic.
A proposal sets out the question, literature review, method, ethics and timetable.
Secondary sources are published writings; primary sources are first-hand materials such as interviews, recordings and the texts you analyse.
Transcription turns recorded speech into text; coding groups repeated ideas into themes.
The project report usually follows a set structure and a consistent reference style.
In the oral defence, explain your question, method, findings and limits, and admit what you do not know.

en.title: Advanced Igbo Phonology and Morphosyntax: Debates and Evidence
en.short: Tone, vowel harmony, word structure and sentence structure debates in Igbo.

sections.heading: Tone and harmony
sections.text:
Igbo is a tone language: pitch distinguishes words and marks grammar. Debate asks how tones are represented.
