Autosegmental phonology treats tone as a separate tier linked to tone-bearing units, so one tone may spread. Analyses differ on downstep: a floating low tone, a register shift, or a phonetic effect? They also differ on grammatical tone in focus and negation. Test an analysis by its predictions: if a high tone should spread rightwards, check every listed environment and ask whether speakers reject the predicted forms.

Vowel harmony is often described as an advanced tongue root (ATR) system. Suffixes may alternate between two vowel sets, but the status of the low vowel and the domain of harmony are disputed. Some treat harmony as root-controlled and word-level; others allow phrase-level effects. A minimal pair in which only the vowel set changes is a test.

sections.heading: Word structure
sections.text: Morphology asks how units build words. Igbo uses prefixes, suffixes, reduplication and compounding. Debates include whether a nominal prefix is a word part or a clitic, how to segment complex verbs, and whether a sequence is a compound or a phrase. If a form can be interrupted by a modifier, that is evidence for a phrase; if it cannot, evidence for a word. Reduplication may mark plurality, intensity or repetition, and analysts disagree on whether it copies a syllable, a stem or a tone pattern. Check productivity and meaning.

sections.heading: Sentence structure
sections.text: Igbo basic clauses are often described as subject-verb-object. Debates concern focus and topic constructions, wh-questions, serial verb constructions and whether a verb phrase exists. One analysis derives focus by movement; another generates it directly. They make different predictions about agreement, tone and position. Serial verbs raise the question of whether two verbs form one predicate or two clauses. Use judgments from several speakers, not one, and compare dialects. If a proposed movement leaves a tone behind, that tone must be accounted for; if not, the analysis is weak.

keyPoints: Igbo tone is lexical and grammatical, and autosegmental analyses link tones to tone-bearing units.
Downstep and grammatical tone are analysed differently, so each account must be tested against speaker judgments.
Vowel harmony is often treated as ATR harmony, but the low vowel and harmony domain remain disputed.
Word-structure debates turn on whether a form is a word, clitic, compound or phrase, and on how reduplication copies material.
Sentence-structure debates concern focus, topic, wh-questions, serial verbs and whether a verb phrase exists.
Evaluate competing analyses by predictions, minimal pairs, several speakers and dialect comparison.

en.title: Advanced Literary Theory and Igbo Criticism
en.short: Critical theory, aesthetics, postcolonial and African literary theory applied to Igbo oral and written texts.

sections.heading: Theory and criticism
sections.text: Literary theory is the systematic study of assumptions behind reading: what a text is, how meaning is made, and what counts as value. Criticism is the practice of interpreting particular texts with those assumptions made clear. Igbo criticism means criticism written in Igbo or about Igbo literature. A master’s reading should name its method, give textual evidence, and admit limits. No single theory owns Igbo literature; formalism, structuralism, reader-response, cultural studies and postcolonial criticism can each ask different questions.

sections.heading: Aesthetics and value
sections.text: Aesthetics is the theory of beauty and artistic value. One debate asks whether standards are universal or culturally grounded. Igbo oral art is often judged by performance: the narrator’s voice, gesture, audience response, repetition and proverbs. Written Igbo texts invite attention to language, plot, character and style. A critic should not import a foreign standard unexamined, nor treat “African” as one taste. The better question is what a text is trying to do and how well it does it.

sections.heading: Postcolonial and African theory
sections.text: Postcolonial criticism studies how colonial power shaped representation, language, education and publishing. Edward Said’s Orientalism (1978) examined Western knowledge about the “East”; Frantz Fanon’s The Wretched of the Earth (1961) analysed colonial psychology and resistance. African literary theory debates decolonisation, universalism and language choice. Chinweizu, Jemie and Madubuike’s Toward the Decolonization of African Literature (1980) attacked Eurocentric standards. Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o’s Decolonising the Mind (1986) argued for writing in African languages. Chinua Achebe defended a usable African English. These positions differ; readers should weigh them.

sections.heading: Applying the theory
sections.text: Apply theory to a concrete case. Suppose a student studies a recorded Igbo folktale in which a small animal outwits a powerful one. A formalist reads plot and repetition; a performance critic asks about the narrator’s gestures and audience; a postcolonial critic asks how recording, transcription and translation changed the tale. For a written Igbo novel, the same student might compare narrative voice with oral storytelling. The strongest work triangulates theory, close reading and context, and states the critic’s own position.

keyPoints: Literary theory makes reading assumptions explicit; criticism applies them to particular texts.
Aesthetic value is debated: universal standards and culturally grounded criteria both need argument.
Igbo oral art is often judged through performance, audience response and verbal art, not text alone.
Postcolonial criticism examines colonial power in representation, language, education and publishing.
African literary theory includes disagreements over decolonisation, universalism and language choice.
A strong reading names its method, uses close textual evidence and notes recording or translation limits.

en.title: Language Planning, Endangerment and Revitalisation of Igbo
en.short: Language policy theory, shift and endangerment, and evidence-based revitalisation of Igbo, including diaspora.

sections.heading: Policy and planning
sections.text: Language policy is the set of official and unofficial decisions about language use. Language planning is deliberate intervention to change those uses. A framework separates status planning, which concerns functions such as education or administration; corpus planning, which concerns form such as spelling and terminology; and acquisition planning, which concerns who learns the language. Kloss is associated with the status and corpus distinction; Cooper added acquisition planning. Test policy claims by asking who decided, who implements, what resources follow, and what outcomes are measured.

sections.heading: Shift and endangerment
sections.text: Language shift is the gradual replacement of one language by another across domains such as home, school, work and worship. Endangerment is not simply a low speaker count. A language with many speakers can be endangered if children stop learning it and domains shrink. Fishman’s Graded Intergenerational Disruption Scale, later expanded as EGIDS, treats transmission between generations as central. Evidence should include domain use, speaker age and whether children speak the language to each other, not only census numbers.

sections.heading: Revitalisation strategies
sections.text: Revitalisation combines status, corpus and acquisition measures. Status measures raise use and prestige, for example in education, media and official services. Corpus measures supply usable resources: standard terms, dictionaries, keyboards and online content. Acquisition measures support learning through teacher training, materials and family programmes. For Igbo, the test is whether these measures increase ordinary use. In the diaspora, heritage classes, churches and online groups can help, but they may produce symbolic identity without conversation. Family language policy is crucial.

sections.heading: Assessing claims
sections.text: Consider an invented case. The Okonkwo family in London speaks Igbo at meals, but the children answer in English, and homework and screens are English. A weekend Igbo class teaches reading. The class supports literacy, yet if the siblings stop speaking Igbo to each other, the home domain is still shifting. A claim that the class is revitalising Igbo needs evidence of increased use outside the classroom. Ask what changed in daily interaction and whether the change lasted.

keyPoints: Language policy is decisions about language use; planning is deliberate intervention.
Status, corpus and acquisition planning address functions, form and learning.
Language shift is replacement across domains; endangerment is shown by failing intergenerational transmission.
Speaker counts alone are weak evidence; domain use and child-to-child use matter.
Revitalisation needs status, corpus and acquisition measures that increase ordinary use.
Diaspora heritage classes can support literacy, but family language policy decides daily transmission.

en.title: Advanced Research Methods and Dissertation Design in Igbo Studies
en.short: Advanced methods, ethics, proposal writing, data analysis and dissertation design for Igbo research.

sections.heading: Designing the study
sections.text: A master’s dissertation answers one clear question with evidence. Start with a research problem, then a question, then a design. A design is the plan that links question, data and analysis. In Igbo studies the question may concern language use, a literary text or cultural practice. Choose methods that fit the question, not methods that are merely fashionable. A mixed methods design combines qualitative and quantitative work; explain how the parts connect.

sections.heading: Methods and example
sections.text:
Qualitative methods explore meaning and context. They include interviews, focus groups, participant observation, archival work and close reading. Sampling is often purposive: you choose people or texts because they can inform the question. Quantitative methods measure patterns. They include surveys, corpus counts, acceptability tests and experiments. Probability sampling gives every member of a population a known chance of selection. Reliability means consistent results; validity means measuring what you claim to measure. Triangulation compares more than one source or method.

Worked example: if 150 questionnaires are sent and 120 return, the response rate is 120 ÷ 150 = 80%. If 72 of the 120 respondents are women, that is 72 ÷ 120 = 60%.

sections.heading: Ethics and analysis
sections.text: Research ethics protects people, communities and knowledge. Seek informed consent, explain purpose and risks, and allow withdrawal. Protect anonymity and data. For oral history or sacred material, ask permission and agree how recordings and names may be used. Analysis must be systematic. Qualitative coding labels segments of data, then groups them into themes. Quantitative analysis uses descriptive statistics first, then tests if the design allows. Report limitations honestly.

sections.heading: Proposal and dissertation
sections.text: A proposal states the question, literature gap, method, ethics, timetable and expected contribution. The dissertation turns this into chapters: introduction, literature review, methodology, analysis, conclusion. Keep an audit trail of decisions. A good dissertation is feasible, ethical and transparent, not merely long.

keyPoints: A dissertation design links one clear research question to data and analysis.
Qualitative methods explore meaning; quantitative methods measure patterns, and mixed methods must explain how they connect.
Probability sampling gives every population member a known chance of selection; purposive sampling selects information-rich cases.
Response rate = returned questionnaires ÷ distributed questionnaires × 100; here 120 ÷ 150 = 80%.
Informed consent, anonymity, data protection and community permission are core ethical requirements.
A proposal must state the question, gap, method, ethics, timetable and expected contribution.
